Israeli passengers arrive at Ben Gurion Airport after flydubai suspension
Israeli passengers stranded in Dubai arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on an Arkia Airlines flight, the first since the Emirati airline flydubai suspended the route and Israel's flag carrier El Al cancelled planned repatriation flights, Reuters reported.
The flights were suspended after an Israel-bound flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on 30 September, after its co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash the plane.
The flydubai flight was travelling from Dubai to Ben Gurion Airport with 180 passengers on board, most of them Israeli.
About an hour before its scheduled arrival, the plane began a steep descent, dropping from 34,000 feet (10,363 metres) to 16,000 feet (4876.8 metres) in less than two minutes.
It eventually landed safely in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

The US has deployed additional Patriot air defence batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar, as President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to resume attacking Iran.
The US sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility and another to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility, Axios reported Thursday.
The deployments are notable because Patriot batteries are in high demand worldwide, and the US has a limited supply. The US has just 33 batteries stationed at home and 27 batteries stationed overseas, according to the nonprofit Missile Defence Alliance.
The US’s allies, including Gulf states like Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, already operate their own batteries, but have relied on Washington for additional protection as they have borne the brunt of Iran’s retaliation for US and Israeli attacks.
Saudi Arabia is in a particularly difficult position with its energy infrastructure and cities coming under attack from Houthi fighters in Yemen and Shia militias in Iraq. France approved 35 new sales of military equipment to Israel between May and September 2026, a new research by rights groups has found.
Jointly investigated by the Palestinian Youth Movement and the French collective Urgence Palestine, the probe documents shipments from French companies to Israel's military, including cooling systems for tanks and missile launchers, helmet visors for helicopter and fighter-jet pilots, connectors and electronic equipment, as well as surveillance systems.
"All were destined for Elbit Systems subsidiaries," the report, seen by Middle East Eye, indicates. Elbit Systems is a leading actor in the Israeli arms industry.
The findings, to be published next week, show that the equipment was manufactured across five regions in France by French companies, including the military conglomerate Thales, which produced and exported control panels used to operate weapons remotely.
These revelations come just months after the two organisations released a first joint investigation in April, which found that France exported more than 525 shipments of military-use equipment to Israel between October 2023 and March 2026.
The April report also documented 117 flights carrying F-35 fighter-jet components departing from Paris's main airport, Roissy-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).
In the new investigation, researchers identified four new suppliers and found that 33 of the 35 shipments passed through CDG airport, of which 32 were transported by Israel's national airline El Al.

Hunger in Yemen is accelerating, with a record number of people unable to meet their food needs as conflict intensifies in the country, the World Food Programme said on Friday.
A record number of people in government-controlled areas of the country where the WFP can access are no longer able to meet their food needs, with three out of four households skipping meals, according to Matthew Hollingworth, the WFP’s assistant executive director for programme operations.
The total population of government-held areas is estimated at around 10 million people.
“The effect of this latest flare-up of insecurity on the food security situation threatens to be absolutely devastating,” Hollingworth told reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome.

Day after day, the Israeli-occupied village of Mansouri, perched on a green hill a few kilometres south of the coastal city of Tyre, is slowly disappearing. Already heavily damaged during the war, it is now quite literally being wiped off the map, in a final twist of cynicism, during the ceasefire.
The Israeli army, which has made it one of its main theatres of operations for weeks, is sparing no effort: demolitions with explosives and air strikes have followed one another at a relentless pace in recent days, to the despair of the village’s roughly 5,000 inhabitants.
The village, which the Israeli army presents as an operational stronghold of Hezbollah, was initially located outside the “Yellow Line”, the “security” demarcation imposed by Israel on Lebanese territory shortly after the latest ceasefire came into effect.
Even then, residents Middle East Eye spoke to following the ceasefire feared that the zone would eventually swallow up their village. It now has, although officially only in part: the Yellow Line cuts through Mansouri, dividing it in two.
On paper, that is, as the village is now entirely occupied – this summer, all the residents who had returned to the area had no choice but to flee once again, under fire from the Israeli air force, which continues its operations.

Who is leading the race for 'the most impossible job on this Earth'?
In April 1953, Norwegian UN Secretary-General Trygve Lie was at New York’s Idlewild Airport to meet his successor. "Welcome, Dag Hammarskjold, to the most impossible job on this Earth," he greeted the Swedish diplomat.
Seven decades later, the UN is about to choose the successor to incumbent Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, for what many regard as one of the trickiest roles on the world stage. Each term lasts five years, usually renewable for a second term.
The next holder of the post is expected to come from Latin America, given how the post rotates between continents (the last Latin American was Peru’s Javier Perez de Cuellar, who left office in 1992). There is also a long-standing, informal push for the UN to appoint a woman for the first time in its 80-year history.
Whoever wins takes on an organisation under strain from multiple directions. Washington, the UN’s biggest contributor, has cut voluntary funding and withdrawn from the World Health Organization (WHO). Elsewhere, worsening financial pressures and unpaid member state contributions have deepened the ongoing liquidity crisis.
Under Guterres, the UN Security Council has been unable to halt or prevent genocides in Gaza and Sudan, or Russia’s war on Ukraine. Furthermore, the US has committed what many regard as breaches of the charter, including abducting and detaining the president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro.
The eight candidates each have their own agenda, but common issues have emerged, including the UN being more proactive to prevent potential crises emerging; the need to be a more streamlined organisation; reducing overlapping functions; allowing smaller nations more opportunity to shake off their debt burdens; and the impact of AI and other technologies on the world.

A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.

With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.

"Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests," the Pentagon said in a statement.
The US first occupied Iraq in 2003, following the overthrow of Hussein, before pulling out its forces in 2011. They returned at the request of the Iraqi government in 2014 to tackle the spread of the Islamic State (IS) militant group, which had seized around a third of the country.
The US began withdrawing troops from Iraq in 2025, with soldiers relocating from Ain al-Asad base in Anbar Province and the Victory Base Complex, located within the Baghdad International Airport, to Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Iraqi Kurdistan was granted some semi-autonomy in 2005. For example, it has its own prime minister, president, and a separate security force, the Peshmerga.

Influential Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr has said the US should compensate Iraqis for the damage inflicted on the country, as the last American troops pull out of Iraq.
In a statement on Wednesday, which is the deadline for American forces to end their 12-year presence in the country, Sadr hailed the "independence of Iraq" and praised those who fought against the US.
"We demand compensation from the American army for all the damages that occurred as a result of its occupation of Iraqi lands," he said.
"Everyone should file legal complaints regarding this."
The US first occupied Iraq in 2003 following the overthrow of Saddam Hussein, before pulling out its forces in 2011.
They returned at the request of the Iraqi government in 2014 to tackle the spread of the Islamic State group, which had seized around a third of the country.
